identification.summary: UAT-8099 is Cisco Talos's designation for a Chinese-speaking cybercrime group focused on SEO fraud and theft of credentials, configuration files and certificate data from reputable, high-value IIS servers [S1][S2]. Talos first identified the group in April 2025 and published its first report on 2025-10-02 [S2][S3]. The group uses web shells, open-source tools, Cobalt Strike and BadIIS malware variants [S2]. A January 2026 Talos follow-up covered region-specific BadIIS variants focused on Vietnam and Thailand [S5][S6].
identification.notes: Talos uses the 'UAT' prefix for an uncategorized cluster; this is a vendor cluster, not a government-attributed actor. Dark Reading notes resemblance to other Chinese-language SEO fraud operations (ESET GhostRedirector, Unit 42 CL-UNK-1037) with unclear boundaries [S3]; these clusters are not merged here. Primary Talos posts could not be opened; details come from secondary coverage.

attribution.confidence: Talos describes the group as Chinese-speaking and financially motivated (cybercrime) [S1][S2]. No state sponsorship is stated in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Talos's 'Chinese-speaking' characterization as reported by secondary coverage [S2][S3]. The specific linguistic or tooling evidence was not visible in the sources gathered.

objectives: SEO fraud (manipulating search rankings by redirecting search-engine crawlers and, in some variants, users) and theft of credentials, configuration files and certificates, which Talos says are packaged for resale or further exploitation [S2][S3].

targeting.notes: Talos file-census and DNS analysis identified affected IIS servers in these countries, targeting organizations such as universities, tech firms and telecom providers [S2][S3]. The January 2026 follow-up emphasized Thailand and Vietnam [S5]. Targeting is of opportunity (vulnerable IIS servers), not of intelligence interest, per the sources.

capabilities.summary: Initial access is via an exploited vulnerability or weak file-upload settings, followed by a web shell for reconnaissance [S5][S2]. The actor enables the guest account, raises it to administrator and enables RDP [S2]. Persistence combines RDP with SoftEther VPN, EasyTier and FRP reverse proxy, and hidden accounts such as admin$ and, when blocked, mysql$ [S2][S5]. GotoHTTP remote-control is launched via a VBScript downloaded by PowerShell after web shell deployment [S5]. Other tools include Sharp4RemoveLog (event log removal), CnCrypt Protect (file hiding) and OpenArk64 (terminating security processes), plus Cobalt Strike [S5][S2]. BadIIS checks whether a visitor is a search crawler and redirects it to an SEO fraud site [S2]. The January 2026 follow-up described variants (IISHijack aimed at Vietnam; asdSearchEngine aimed at Thailand or Thai-language users, injecting a JavaScript redirect), three variants within the asdSearchEngine cluster, and signs of a refined Linux BadIIS version [S5][S6].

campaigns.summary: Talos reports activity (start date reported inconsistently, from August or late 2025, into early 2026) focused mainly on Thailand and Vietnam, with region-specific BadIIS variants, hidden-account fallback (admin$ to mysql$) and a refined Linux BadIIS.

diamond.adversary: Chinese-speaking, financially motivated cybercrime group tracked by Talos as UAT-8099 [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Web shells, PowerShell/VBScript, GotoHTTP, Cobalt Strike, BadIIS variants, SoftEther VPN, EasyTier, FRP, and anti-forensic tools [S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised IIS servers used to serve SEO-fraud redirects; the sources gathered do not detail C2 or hosting.
diamond.victim: Reputable IIS servers at universities, tech firms and telecom providers in India, Thailand, Vietnam, Canada and Brazil [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial motive (search-ranking manipulation and resale of stolen credentials); no state tasking stated in the sources [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing Microsoft IIS servers with exploitable vulnerabilities or weak file-upload settings [S5][S2].

gaps: Primary Talos posts (October 2025 and January 2026) could not be opened; findings rely on secondary coverage, so specific IOCs, CVEs and exact dates for the follow-up are unverified [S1][S4].
Initial-access vulnerabilities are described only generically (exploited vulnerability or weak file upload); specific CVEs are not known from the sources gathered.
The basis for the 'Chinese-speaking' assessment and any confidence level are not visible in the sources gathered.
Relationship to ESET GhostRedirector [S7][S8] and Unit 42 CL-UNK-1037 is unresolved; Dark Reading says the boundaries are murky [S3].
No MITRE ATT&CK group or Microsoft name was found; no state links are asserted.
Exact publication date of the January 2026 follow-up is unverified (month only).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing IIS servers at universities, telecoms and tech firms (including mission partners and DoD-adjacent contractors) are exposed terrain; the group's effect is reputational and credential exposure rather than mission disruption [S2][S3]. STEP 2: The actor is opportunistic and criminal, with automation to evade defenses, so it targets any vulnerable server regardless of owner [S2]. STEP 3: Template is exploit or weak upload, web shell, recon, guest-to-admin account, RDP, VPN/proxy persistence, hidden accounts, then BadIIS and credential/certificate theft [S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued SEO fraud across IIS servers in South and Southeast Asia and the Americas. MDCOA is resale of harvested credentials and certificates to other actors, giving them footholds in partner networks (an inference from Talos's note on resale [S2]). Candidate indicators: hidden accounts ending in $ (admin$, mysql$), unexpected SoftEther/EasyTier/FRP/GotoHTTP binaries, event-log clearing, and IIS modules returning different content to crawlers [S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track IIS exposure on partner and contractor networks, especially in Thailand, Vietnam and India, where activity is reported [S2][S5]. (2) Authorities: remediation of non-DoD or partner-owned servers falls to owners; coordinate through established channels (e.g., DC3/DIB CS for contractors) rather than direct action. (3) Mission assurance: stolen certificates and credentials from compromised servers could be reused against connected systems, so prioritize credential and certificate rotation after any compromise [S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partners; Talos published the reporting, but IOCs should be taken from the primary posts [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: UAT-8099 is a Chinese-speaking cybercrime group primarily engaged in SEO fraud and the theft of high-value credentials, configuration files, and certificate data from vulnerable IIS servers. They utilize web shells and PowerShell to deploy the GotoHTTP tool for remote access, while also employing techniques such as DLL sideloading and RDP for persistence. The group has been observed using BadIIS variants for SEO manipulation and executing reconnaissance commands to gather system information. Additionally, they create hidden accounts and utilize VPN tools to maintain long-term access to compromised systems.
